Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is a gastrointestinal motility disorder that results from the reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus or oral cavity resulting in symptoms or complications. The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of gastric contents into the oropharynx. GERD affects quality of life and may cause erosive esophagitis, esophageal strictures, and Barrett esophagus, a precursor to esophageal adenocarcinoma. GERD is a clinical diagnosis and is most effectively treated with proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs). Long-term use of PPIs is associated with bone fractures, chronic renal disease, acute renal disease, community-acquired pneumonia, and Clostridium difficile intestinal infection.

Gastroesophageal reflux (GER) in children is very common and refers to the involuntary passage of gastric contents into the esophagus. This is often physiological and managed conservatively. In contrast, GER disease (GERD) is a less common pathologic process causing troublesome symptoms, which may need medical management. Apart from abnormal transient relaxations of the lower esophageal sphincter, other factors that play a role in the pathogenesis of GERD include defects in esophageal mucosal defense, impaired esophageal and gastric motility and clearance, as well as anatomical defects of the lower esophageal reflux barrier such as hiatal hernia. The clinical manifestations of GERD in young children are varied and nonspecific prompting the necessity for careful diagnostic evaluation. Management should be targeted to the underlying aetiopathogenesis and to limit complications of GERD. The following review focuses on up-to-date information regarding of the pathogenesis, diagnostic evaluation and management of GERD in children.

Symptoms potentially attributable to gastroesophageal reflux disease are among those most commonly reported to primary care providers in the outpatient setting. In this review, we discuss clinical approaches to the evaluation and management of these symptoms, including proton pump inhibitor trials as well as specific indications or clinical settings that warrant referral to Gastroenterology specialists.

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the back of the throat [18#0]. GERD happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#1]. It can hurt your quality of life and may lead to serious problems like inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and a condition called Barrett esophagus, which can develop into esophageal cancer [18#2]. In children, GERD is less common than simple reflux and causes troublesome symptoms that may need medical treatment [19#3]. Factors that contribute to GERD include problems with the esophageal sphincter not closing properly, weak defenses in the esophageal lining, poor movement and clearing of the esophagus and stomach, and physical defects like a hiatal hernia [19#4]. The most effective treatment is a class of drugs called proton-pump inhibitors, but long-term use carries risks including bone fractures, kidney disease, pneumonia, and intestinal infection [18#5][18#6].

data.narrative: The typical symptoms of GERD are heartburn and regurgitation of stomach contents into the throat [18#0]. The condition happens when stomach contents flow back into the esophagus or mouth, causing symptoms or complications [18#1]. GERD can lead to serious problems including inflammation of the esophagus, narrowing of the esophagus, and Barrett esophagus, which can precede esophageal cancer [18#2]. Risk factors and underlying causes include abnormal relaxation of the valve between the stomach and esophagus, weakness in the esophageal lining's defenses, poor movement and clearing of the esophagus and stomach, and anatomical defects such as hiatal hernia [19#3]. In children, the symptoms can be varied and nonspecific, requiring careful evaluation [19#4]. These symptoms are among the most commonly reported to primary care providers [20#5]. The condition is known by the name Gastroesophageal reflux (GERD) in MedGen [2] and as Gastroesophageal Reflux in the literature [3]. Multiple PubMed articles are titled Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease [1][6][9][15]. One article is titled Gastroesophageal reflux disease in children: What's new right now? [12]. Several clinical trials are studying GERD treatments, including famotidine for non-erosive GERD [4], pantoprazole for acid reflux symptoms in adults [7], the natural history of GER in children and adolescents [10], on-demand treatment of reflux disease [13], and endoscopic fundoplication as a placebo-controlled treatment [16]. The PubMed publications related to GERD include pmid 29132520 [5], pmid 33351044 [8], pmid 36170502 [11], pmid 37034973 [14], and pmid 37516506 [17].
